warmup.text: Isaac's family is walking with Gabe, Ruth and their little girl, Nita. Nita is five, and she has something to ask Isaac. The poem today has an I in it, but that I is not the poet. Keep that in mind. A voice in a poem or a story can belong to someone the writer made.

words.text: You met the life root and the breath root. Now decide which one is hiding in each word. Some words carry both ideas. Then sort the describing words by their endings. Find the smaller word inside first. Then the footprint game has six new words to build.

reading.text: Read Chapter 9 in your book. Watch what Isaac promises, and what he does the next morning to keep that promise. Then read the Read Like a Writer sentence and notice how Isaac lets you inside his head. Finish with the Virtue Watch at the end of this tab.

assignment.text: Three questions about Chapter 9, then a first draft. Write three to five sentences about the conflict you planned. Let the tension build, and do not solve the problem yet. Copy your work into Canvas when you finish.

do: Read today's skill.
Tap the lens you will use today.
Watch who can see the ghost walkers and who cannot.
how.why: When two people look at the same thing, their perspectives show.
how.use: You will use this for the chapter questions.

do: Tap the highlighted words in the first sentence.
Fix the second sentence out loud.
Tap Check My Work to compare.
how.why: Commas after an opening phrase or clause tell the reader where to pause.

do: Read the poem out loud once.
Read Think About It.
Keep your answer in mind as you read.
how.why: Knowing who is speaking, and that it may not be the writer, helps you understand any poem or story.

do: Ask: is this word about life or about breath?
Tap a word, then tap its root.
Match all four.
how.why: Finding the root tells you what a long word is about.

do: Read each sentence from the book.
Look for clues around the word.
Tap a word, then tap its meaning.
how.why: Clues in a sentence can tell you what a word means.

do: Look for was, were or by.
Tap the sentence that hides who acted.
Rewrite all three in the box.
how.why: A passive sentence can leave out who did the action. Noticing that makes you a sharper reader.

do: Find the smaller word inside each describing word.
Tap a word, then tap its column.
how.why: The ending a word takes often depends on its base.

do: Read Chapter 9 first.
Answer each question in 2 or more sentences.
Use details from the chapter as evidence.
how.why: These questions check what happened and what it shows about the people on the road.

do: Look at your Day 1 notes.
Write 3 to 5 sentences about the conflict.
Start one sentence with a transition or a when clause, then a comma.
Do not solve the problem yet.
how.why: Rising action means the tension climbs. Leaving it unsolved keeps your reader reading.
how.use: Next lesson you will revise this draft.

do: Read what perseverance means.
Read the example from this week.
After you read, fill in your perseverance log at the end of this tab.
Read the chapter introduction below.
Open your book and read Chapter 9.
Then do the Virtue Watch and the Read Like a Writer box below.

glossary.meaning: the voice talking in a poem, which may not be the poet
the way a person sees what is happening, based on what they have lived through

miss.creative: Find create inside. The silent e drops, then -ive: creative.
miss.dramatic: Find drama inside. It takes -ic, with a t: dramatic.
miss.national: Find nation inside. It takes -al: national.
miss.poetic: Find poet inside. It takes -ic: poetic.
miss.secretive: Find secret inside. It takes -ive: secretive.
miss.supportive: Find support inside. It takes -ive: supportive.
miss.survival: Find survive inside. The silent e drops, then -al: survival.
miss.symbolic: Find symbol inside. It takes -ic: symbolic.
miss.traditional: Find tradition inside. It takes -al: traditional.

game.title: Footprints Forward
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 footprints today
game.look: Isaac's family walks for days on a snowy road. In this game, each footprint in the snow holds a word. Pick the ending, -ive, -al or -ic, that turns it into a describing word, and the footprint lights up. Your walk keeps going all week.

do: Read the word on the footprint.
Say it with each ending.
Tap the ending that makes a real describing word.
Tap Next footprint.
how.why: These are the same three endings from Spelling, with new words. If you can build a word you have never practiced, you know the endings.

steps.why: Yes: scene + -ic = scenic. The silent e drops.

art.title: Winter Sunset in a Spruce Forest
art.alt: A painting of a snowy spruce forest with a warm orange sunset glowing between the dark trunks.
art.look: Julius Klever painted this forest in Russia in 1889. It is far from Isaac's road, but it feels like Chapter 9: the cold all around, and one warm light where the families gather at the end of the day.
art.lookBtn: Tap to learn about this painting
art.creator: Julius Klever

cards.title: Choctaw words in Chapters 8 and 9
cards.intro: Isaac tells his story in English, but some Choctaw words stay in it.

items.meaning: Hello. Isaac's family says it to Nita when they meet her in Chapter 8.
Thank you. Isaac explains it in Chapter 9.
Choctaw corn soup, made with soft corn in milk.
items.line: We had Choctaw corn soup for supper that night. Pashofa, we call it.

cards.note: The narrator does not say these words aloud. Choctaw has its own sounds, and we would rather not teach them wrong.

virtue.name: perseverance
virtue.title: My perseverance log
virtue.intro: Chapter 9 has moments where people keep going. Tap the one you think took the most perseverance.

options.t: Isaac stands up at the campfire and promises Nita, “I will take care of you.”
Isaac cuts two pieces from his own blanket and ties them on Nita's feet as shoes.
The rain turns to ice, and the families walk all day without stopping, with nothing to eat.

virtue.line: Finish the sentence: It took perseverance because…
